LA Times Editorial Supports Restrictions On Prop 215, But Says,
"Washington's all out ban on the medical use of marijuana is needlessly stringent."

August 16, 1999
From The Los Angeles Times
letters@latimes.com
http://www.latimes.com
http://www.latimes.com/home/discuss

PUT WISE CONTROLS ON POT LAW

See
California Governor Now Expected To Veto Vasconcellos’
Medical Marijuana Patient Registration Bill;
Committee Appropriates $1 Million For UC To Study Medical Marijuana.
and
California Taskforce On Prop 215 Reportedly Recommends Registration System
To Protect Patients Against Rogue Law Enforcement

Gov. Gray Davis has suggested he will veto a bill that lays out details for implementing Proposition 215, the controversial initiative that voters passed in 1996 to legalize the medical use of marijuana. Davis spokesman Michael Bustamante said the governor would be "hard pressed" to sign the bill, by state Sen. John Vasconcellos (D-Santa Clara), because it would put California in the position of legalizing a drug that the federal government bans altogether.

Davis' veto wouldn't settle a thing. California would still be stuck with a vague law impossible to put into effect.
(Marijuananews note: Prop 215 is not "impossible to put into effect." It is working well in San Francisco, Oakland, and other areas. The only problem is that law enforcement will not obey the law in much of California.)
See
Full Text of Proposition 215 Compassionate Use Act of 1996

What Davis ought to do is work with Vasconcellos to tighten the bill's description of legal uses of marijuana and make it more palatable to moderates including himself.

A real solution will require a change in federal drug laws, but a well-crafted bill would help state law enforcement officials as they try to decide what to allow.

Washington's all out ban on the medical use of marijuana is needlessly stringent. While most experts agree that marijuana can alleviate pain and nausea in patients suffering from life threatening diseases like AIDS and cancer, federal law still classifies marijuana as a Schedule 1 drug, meaning a substance without medicinal value. Drugs arguably more dangerous, like morphine and cocaine, by contrast may be prescribed as Schedule 2 drugs.

Davis' veto wouldn't settle a thing. California would still be stuck with a vague law impossible to put into effect.

Washington's all out ban on the medical use of marijuana is needlessly stringent. Drugs arguably more dangerous, like morphine and cocaine, by contrast may be prescribed as Schedule 2 drugs.

Two revisions to the Vasconcellos measure are key:

* Tighten wording. The bill is almost as irresponsibly open ended as Proposition 215, legalizing the use of pot not only for AIDS and cancer but for many lesser conditions. Proposition 215 was sold to voters as a way of helping people cope with grave illnesses; that's how it should be implemented.
(Marijuananews note: Why shouldn’t medical marijuana be used for any condition for which any of the more dangerous pharmaceuticals can be taken.)
See
Forbes Data: "What you don't know can kill you." Which Drugs Kill the Most People?
and
Deadly Drug Sold by Founder of Partnership for A Drug-Free America, Says Forbes

* Limit scope. Most Californians who supported Proposition 215 no doubt assumed that seriously ill people who smoke marijuana would do so discreetly. But Vasconcellos' bill wrongly seeks to permit public smoking of medicinal marijuana just about everywhere cigarettes can be legally smoked.
See
Sacramento Bee Editorial Calls for Ordinance Forbidding Medical Marijuana Use In Public -- In the Closet Perhaps?

The debate over Proposition 215 has officials in Sacramento and Washington in a standoff. Federal drug czar Barry McCaffrey has derided the initiative as "a Cheech and Chong show" that approves of drug use. Vasconcellos has snapped back that "the federal government is so hysterical and unresponsive on this issue that I am not going to let them dictate policy."
See
Drug Czar’s Statement On California SB 848 Is Finally Online –
Maybe They Just Sobered Up After The Alcohol Lobby’s Parties.
and
"The general’s statement, issued on Tuesday, is so rife with inaccuracies,
including selective citations of the Institute of Medicine report his office commissioned,
that it is difficult to take it seriously." Orange County Register Editorial
Davis, rather than pull out his veto pen, should work with the Legislature. A carefully monitored, tightly limited implementation of Proposition 215 would be the best first step.
